words.definition: To develop and flourish into something fuller or more attractive.
words.example: Under her mentor's guidance, the shy intern blossomed into a confident leader.
words.mnemonic: Picture a tight 'blob' of bud that suddenly bursts open — bl-ossom opening wide.

words.definition: The peak period of flowering, growth, or full development.
words.example: The Renaissance marked an efflorescence of art, science, and philosophy across Europe.
words.mnemonic: 'Ef-FLOR-escence' — the FLORa hitting its fullest flower.

words.definition: Green and covered with lush vegetation.
words.example: After the monsoon, the once-dusty hills turned verdant and cool.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'verde' — Spanish and Italian for green.

words.definition: Relating to or occurring in the spring.
words.example: The vernal thaw sent meltwater rushing down every mountain stream.
words.mnemonic: Think of the vernal equinox in March — 'vernal' tags the season of spring.

words.definition: To make or become faster, or to stir into life.
words.example: Her pulse quickened as the footsteps drew closer in the dark.
words.mnemonic: 'Quick' + en — to make quick, the instant something springs to life.

words.definition: To reach full maturity or readiness, especially fruit.
words.example: We left the green tomatoes on the windowsill to ripen in the sun.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rip in' — you can rip into the fruit once it's ready.

words.definition: To encourage the growth or development of something.
words.example: Small discussion groups foster a sense of belonging among new students.
words.mnemonic: A 'foster' parent raises a child not their own — foster means help something grow.

words.definition: To care for and encourage the growth of someone or something.
words.example: Good teachers nurture curiosity instead of merely demanding answers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'nurse' — a nurse tends to something so it grows strong.

words.definition: To prepare land for crops, or to develop something carefully over time.
words.example: Over the years he cultivated a wide network of loyal clients.
words.mnemonic: Root of 'culture' — you tend and grow it, whether soil or a following.

words.definition: To make something larger or greater by adding to it.
words.example: He took a second job to augment his modest salary.
words.mnemonic: Think 'augmented reality' — extra layers added onto what's already there.

words.definition: To increase the strength, volume, or intensity of something.
words.example: Social media can amplify a single complaint into a national outcry.
words.mnemonic: An 'amplifier' makes a guitar louder — amplify means crank it up.

words.definition: To grow quickly and steadily in size, seriousness, or scope.
words.example: A minor disagreement over parking began to escalate until the neighbors stopped speaking entirely.
words.mnemonic: Think of an escalator carrying you steadily upward — things that escalate keep rising.

words.definition: To swell outward because of pressure building from within.
words.example: After the feast, his stomach began to distend until his belt no longer fit.
words.mnemonic: From Latin dis- + tendere, 'to stretch apart' — a full balloon stretches its skin outward.

words.definition: To become wider, more open, or fully expanded.
words.example: When she stepped from the bright street into the dark theater, her pupils began to dilate.
words.mnemonic: Root di- + Latin latus, 'wide' — the eye doctor's drops make pupils go wide.

words.definition: To rot and break apart into simpler chemical substances.
words.example: The gardener buried the scraps so they would decompose and enrich the soil by spring.
words.mnemonic: de- (undo) + compose — it's the undoing of something built, back into raw pieces.

words.definition: To crumble and rot slowly from age and neglect.
words.example: The abandoned library was left to molder, its pages curling and gray with damp.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'mold' + 'older' — old bread grows mold and slowly molders away.

words.definition: To rot and give off a foul, offensive odor.
words.example: The forgotten fish began to putrefy, and the smell drove everyone from the kitchen.
words.mnemonic: Latin root putr- ('rotten') + -fy ('make') — literally 'to make rotten'.

words.definition: Decayed, spoiled, and giving off a disgusting smell.
words.example: One whiff of the putrid meat told them the refrigerator had failed days ago.
words.mnemonic: Say 'PU!' — the sound you make holding your nose — then '-trid'.

words.definition: In the process of rotting and starting to give off a foul stench.
words.example: The swamp air was thick and putrescent, heavy with the odor of dead leaves and mud.
words.mnemonic: putr- ('rotten') + -escent ('becoming'), like fluorescent — this is 'becoming rotten'.

words.definition: To become infected and inflamed, or to steadily grow worse.
words.example: The tiny splinter he ignored began to fester, and by morning his thumb was red and throbbing.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'pester' — an untreated wound keeps pestering you and gets worse.

words.definition: Spoiled, with the sour smell or taste of stale fat or oil.
words.example: The butter had gone rancid, leaving a bitter, greasy film on the toast.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rank acid' — old oil turns rank and sharply sour.

words.definition: To dry out and contract into wrinkles.
words.example: Left too long in the sun, the grapes began to shrivel into wrinkled little raisins.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'shrink' — a shriveled grape shrinks and crinkles into a raisin.

words.definition: To droop and lose firmness, usually from heat or lack of water.
words.example: By noon the freshly cut daisies began to wilt, their heads bowing over the vase's rim.
words.mnemonic: A thirsty flower has lost its 'will' — wi-l-t — and simply flops over.

words.definition: Worn out, weak, or broken down from old age or long, hard use.
words.example: The decrepit farmhouse sagged on its foundations, its shutters hanging by a single rusted hinge.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'the CREPT-in' — so old and feeble it can barely creep in the door.

words.definition: The state of being weak and broken down from old age or long neglect.
words.example: Years of poverty and illness had reduced the once-proud manor, and its owner, to utter decrepitude.
words.mnemonic: 'decrepit' + '-tude' — the -tude ending turns the crumbling adjective into the condition itself.

words.definition: Fallen into partial ruin or disrepair through age or neglect.
words.example: Squatters had moved into the dilapidated tenement, sleeping beneath a ceiling that leaked at every seam.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'lapis' (stone) — literally the stones falling out of a wall, like a de-LAP-idated building shedding rocks.

words.definition: The gradual process of growing old and declining in function.
words.example: The biologist studied why some cells enter senescence and stop dividing while their neighbors keep multiplying.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'senior' and 'senile' — 'sen-' always means old.

words.definition: Growing old; declining or deteriorating with advancing age.
words.example: The senescent oak dropped fewer acorns each autumn, its hollow trunk home only to owls.
words.mnemonic: 'sen-' (old, as in senior) + '-escent' (becoming, as in adolescent) — becoming old.

words.definition: To make or become smaller, weaker, or less in amount.
words.example: As the medication took hold, the throbbing in her temples began to diminish until it was barely noticeable.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'mini' — to diminish is to make things more mini.

words.definition: To drain or weaken someone's strength, energy, or resolve gradually.
words.example: The relentless heat sapped the marchers until they could barely lift their feet.
words.mnemonic: A tree bleeds out its sap and grows weak — draining the sap drains the life.

words.definition: To seriously weaken the strength or energy of a person or thing.
words.example: The fever debilitated him so thoroughly that climbing a single flight of stairs left him breathless.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'de-BILITY' from 'ability' — stripping away someone's ability, leaving debility.

words.definition: Abnormally thin and wasted from hunger, illness, or lack of nourishment.
words.example: The rescued dog was so emaciated that every rib pressed sharply against its dull, matted coat.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'macer' (lean) — think 'e-MACE-iated,' skinny enough to swing like a thin mace.

words.definition: Something that spoils, damages, or destroys, especially a plant disease or spreading decay.
words.example: A creeping blight swept through the potato fields, turning healthy leaves black within days.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'night' — a dark blight falls over crops like a sudden killing night.

words.definition: A spreading sore or source of corruption that slowly destroys from within.
words.example: Greed spread through the company like a canker, rotting its values long before the scandal broke.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'cancer' — both come from Latin 'cancer' (crab), an eating, spreading ulcer.

words.definition: Having lost strength, energy, or the ability to be effective.
words.example: Years of easy luxury had left the once-fierce dynasty effete, unable to defend its own borders.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'eh-FEET' — feet so tired and weak they can't perform a single feat anymore.

words.definition: To remove all moisture from something, leaving it completely dry.
words.example: The scorching desert wind will desiccate any fruit left uncovered within a few hours.
words.mnemonic: 'de-SICC-ate' — Latin siccus means dry; the sun makes it sick until bone dry.

words.definition: To dry out from heat, or make someone extremely thirsty.
words.example: A long march under the blazing sun left the soldiers' throats parched and cracking.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a 'porch' baking in the summer heat until everything on it is cracked-dry.

words.definition: Twisted, knotted, and rough, as from age or hard weather.
words.example: The old sailor's gnarled hands gripped the rope, every knuckle swollen from decades at sea.
words.mnemonic: 'Gnarly' old tree — full of knots and twists, its bark knurled and lumpy.

words.definition: Too old to be useful or effective; retired or outdated because of age.
words.example: The office still ran a superannuated computer that no modern software could even install on.
words.mnemonic: super + annus (Latin 'year') — piled up with so many years it's been put out to pasture.

words.definition: The process of falling out of use as something newer replaces it.
words.example: Planned obsolescence ensures each phone slows down just as the next model hits the shelves.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'obsolete essence' — the very essence of a thing no longer being wanted.

words.definition: Gradually passing out of use and heading toward being outdated.
words.example: By the late 1990s the fax machine was clearly obsolescent, though many offices clung to it.
words.mnemonic: The '-escent' ending means 'in the process of' — like an adolescent, but becoming extinct.

words.definition: To reduce the force, strength, or thickness of something.
words.example: Thick lead walls attenuate the radiation until it is finally safe to approach the core.
words.mnemonic: 'a-TEN-u-ate' hides 'tenuous' — make it thin and slight.

words.definition: To use up or greatly reduce the amount of something available.
words.example: Decades of overfishing have depleted the cod stocks that once seemed inexhaustible.
words.mnemonic: de- (away) + -plete (fill, as in 'replete') — to un-fill, to empty out.

words.definition: To strip something of its covering, protection, or natural growth.
words.example: Clear-cutting denuded the hillside, leaving raw soil to wash away in the first heavy rains.
words.mnemonic: de + nude — to make nude, to strip it bare.

words.definition: To wear away or scrape off a surface through rubbing or friction.
words.example: The rope, dragged over the same rock ledge for years, was abraded down to a few frayed threads.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'a blade' scraping across a surface — same root as 'abrasive'.

words.definition: To erase or wipe out, making something no longer visible.
words.example: Centuries of wind had effaced the inscription until the tombstone was completely blank.
words.mnemonic: ef + face — rub the 'face' right off the surface.

words.definition: To break apart into small pieces, or slowly fall into ruin.
words.example: The ancient wall crumbled at a touch, the mortar turning to dust between the bricks.
words.mnemonic: Think 'crumbs' — like an apple crumble, it falls apart into little pieces.

words.definition: To dull the shine of metal, or to damage a good reputation.
words.example: A single scandal was enough to tarnish a career built over decades.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tar' + 'varnish' — tar smeared over bright varnish leaves it dull and stained.

words.definition: To spoil something by introducing a trace of contamination or corruption.
words.example: Rumors of bribery taint every decision the committee makes.
words.mnemonic: 'Taint' hides 'ain't' — once it's spoiled, it ain't clean anymore.

words.definition: To confuse someone's thinking, or to cause an egg to go rotten.
words.example: Too little sleep can addle your brain until simple sums feel impossible.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'muddle' — an addled mind is a muddled one.

words.definition: To cause milk to thicken and separate into lumps, especially when soured.
words.example: A squeeze of lemon juice will curdle warm milk within seconds.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'curd' — cheese curds form when milk goes this way.

words.definition: To undergo a chemical change driven by yeast or bacteria, often producing alcohol.
words.example: Leave the grape juice in the sealed barrel and it will ferment into wine.
words.mnemonic: 'Ferment' echoes 'fervent' — picture a fervent, bubbling vat of activity.

words.definition: To sink into a worse state, or to pass duties down to another party.
words.example: The calm debate quickly devolved into shouting and name-calling.
words.mnemonic: The opposite of 'evolve' — 'de-' means down, so things wind downward.

words.definition: To multiply or swarm rapidly, filling a place with teeming life.
words.example: In the stagnant pond, mosquito larvae pullulate through the summer heat.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pullet' (a young hen) + 'populate' — chicks populating everywhere.

words.definition: To bear fruit, or to make an effort productive and rewarding.
words.example: Years of patient research finally fructified into a working vaccine.
words.mnemonic: 'Fruct' is Latin for fruit (as in fructose) — to turn something into fruit.

words.definition: The point at which a plan or effort is fully achieved.
words.example: After a decade of saving, their dream of a bakery finally came to fruition.
words.mnemonic: Rooted in 'fruit' — your long labor at last bears fruit and ripens.

words.definition: To grow or increase very quickly in size or number.
words.example: What began as a garage hobby mushroomed into a global company.
words.mnemonic: Picture a mushroom cloud billowing outward — sudden, rapid expansion.

words.definition: To grow larger in size, volume, or number, often gradually.
words.example: The river began to swell as the rain fell for a third straight day.
words.mnemonic: An ocean swell rises and bulges — the sound and image of growing bulk.

words.definition: To increase quickly to a large size or amount.
words.example: Medical bills can balloon into tens of thousands after a long hospital stay.
words.mnemonic: Picture a party balloon blowing up fast — rapid, visible inflation.

words.definition: Loose debris or waste left behind after destruction, decay, or use.
words.example: After the festival, volunteers cleared the detritus of cups and wrappers from the field.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'debris' crossed with 'detrition' (wearing away) — worn-down leftover bits.

words.definition: The dry outer covering of a seed or grain, or an empty outer shell.
words.example: She peeled back the husk to reveal the golden kernels of corn.
words.mnemonic: 'Husk' and 'hull' both start with h — the dry jacket wrapped around a seed.

words.definition: Easily broken into small fragments or reduced to powder.
words.example: The dried clay was so friable that it fell apart between her fingers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fry-able' — food fried to a crisp crumbles apart at a touch.

words.definition: Having a stale, damp, or moldy smell from age or lack of air.
words.example: The old library books gave off a musty odor of forgotten decades.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'dusty' — picture a dusty, unopened attic thick with damp air.

words.definition: Smelling stale and stuffy; also rigidly old-fashioned in outlook.
words.example: He rejected every new idea, clinging to fusty rules from another century.
words.mnemonic: Blend of 'fussy' and 'dusty' — a fussy old man in a dusty, airless study.

words.definition: Extremely thin and bony, often from hunger, illness, or hardship.
words.example: After months lost at sea, the sailor returned gaunt, his cheeks sunken and hollow.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gone' — so much flesh is gone that only bone remains.

words.definition: Looking exhausted and unwell, especially from stress or lack of sleep.
words.example: Three sleepless nights with the newborn left her haggard and hollow-eyed.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'hag' — a worn, wild-eyed witch drained by too many sleepless nights.

words.definition: Resembling a corpse in being pale, thin, and deathly in appearance.
words.example: His cadaverous pallor made the nurses fear he would not last the night.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'cadaver' (corpse) — imagine a face like one laid out on a slab.

words.definition: Pale and spindly, or weakened, from growing without enough sunlight.
words.example: The seedlings grew etiolated in the dark closet, leggy and ghostly white.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'eat-no-light' — a plant starved of light turns pale and stretched thin.

words.definition: Abandoned and left to fall into ruin; also failing in one's duty.
words.example: Squatters now sheltered inside the derelict factory's crumbling shell.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (away) + 'relinquish' — something relinquished and left to rot.

words.definition: Loosely held together and likely to collapse; badly built or run-down.
words.example: The ramshackle barn swayed and groaned with every gust of wind.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'ram' shaking a 'shack' until it's on the verge of falling down.

words.definition: The return of something harmful after a period of calm or inactivity.
words.example: Doctors feared a recrudescence of the fever once the medication was stopped.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + Latin 'crudus' (raw) — an old wound turning raw once more.

words.definition: To gradually melt or dissolve by absorbing moisture from the surrounding air.
words.example: Left uncapped overnight, the tablets of road salt began to deliquesce into a slick puddle on the shelf.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'delicious' + 'liquesce' — imagine a sugar cube going 'de-LIQUID' as it slowly turns to syrup in the humid air.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — growth and decay
